rust.error: document type declarations are not supported

reason: fast-xml-parser reads a document type declaration and expands the internal entities it declares; that reader (DocTypeReader.js with xml-naming and is-unsafe, about 400 lines) is not ported. Rust refuses the fragment, and that is the decided end state: the Open Packaging Conventions forbid DTDs in a package part. No tracked document has a DOCTYPE in a part the engine parses.

rust.error: a surrogate pair would be split

reason: fast-xml-parser takes the nine UTF-16 units after any '<![' as the CDATA opener, so a malformed opener can cut a character outside the BMP in half and leave a lone surrogate in the text. A Rust string cannot hold a lone surrogate. Rust refuses the fragment instead of inventing a replacement character.

JSZip has two UTF-8 decoders. Where a global Buffer exists (Node: CLI, tests, main process) it replaces each ill-formed sequence with U+FFFD, which is what Rust does and what the gate compares. Where none exists (a browser, and the sandboxed desktop renderer unless a bundler supplies one) it uses pako's decoder, which never rejects a byte: stray continuation bytes become control characters, a lead byte swallows the bytes after it, encoded surrogates stay lone surrogates, and the result depends on where JSZip's 16 KiB blocks end. The TypeScript engine therefore already reads ill-formed parts differently per host. Rust follows the Node behaviour everywhere. Every .xml and .rels entry of the tracked documents is well-formed UTF-8, so no tracked document is affected.

The TypeScript tables are plain objects, so a lookup by a value from the document also answers to the keys every object inherits: __proto__ gives Object.prototype, and constructor, toString, valueOf and hasOwnProperty give functions. A caller that tests the result for truth then stores it: directPLayer sets the paragraph align to it for a w:jc whose w:val is constructor. The Rust tables answer only to their own keys. The gate leaves these keys out of the two table comparisons and checks them here.
See table-lookup-inherited-key-object. A function result is invisible in JSON, which is how a parsed model would lose the field without a trace.
See table-lookup-inherited-key-object: the same lookup on the East Asian default font table.

typescript.refused: zip rejected: part word/styles.xml cannot be inflated: TypeError

rust.refused: zip rejected: part word/styles.xml cannot be inflated: the deflate data is damaged or cut short

reason: The zip gate ends this message with the text of the error DecompressionStream rejects with. That text belongs to the host: Node 22 rejects with a TypeError whose message is empty, so the gate falls back to its name, and a browser words it differently. Rust writes one sentence of its own. The gate compares the message up to "cannot be inflated:", which is the part the TypeScript wrote.

container: zip64 extensible data that reads itself again

rust.refused: Corrupted zip: the ZIP64 extensible data does not end

reason: JSZip 3.10.1 reads the extensible data of a ZIP64 end record in a loop whose counter never advances (zipEntries.js, readBlockZip64EndOfCentral): it ends when a read runs past the data. A field whose length is -6 moves the reader back to the start of the field, so the loop reads the same six bytes for ever and loadDocxZip never returns. The zip gate does not stop the archive: it refuses ZIP64 by the record count, the directory size and offset, and a locator 20 bytes before the end record, while JSZip also takes a disk number of 0xffff as ZIP64 and finds the locator anywhere. Rust refuses the container. This is a defect of the TypeScript engine (a document that hangs the application), reported with unit 1c, not behaviour to reproduce.

container: zip64 extensible data that leads back over two fields

rust.refused: Corrupted zip: the ZIP64 extensible data does not end

reason: The same loop as zip64-extensible-data-never-ends, entered another way: a field of length 0 followed by one of length -12 that ends where the first began. No single field ends where it started, so a reader that only compares a field's end with its own start reads the two for ever, as JSZip does. Rust keeps the starts of the fields it has read and refuses the container at the first one it meets again. Listed apart from the one-field container because the first Rust port refused that one and still hung on this one.

See table-lookup-inherited-key-object. parseStyles lower-cases the w:lang w:eastAsia of the docDefaults and looks it up in EA_LANG_DEFAULT_FONT. For constructor (and __proto__) the TypeScript takes the inherited member for a font: it stores a function as eastAsiaFont and sets eaFromLang. The lower-casing keeps toString, valueOf and hasOwnProperty out. The Rust table answers for its own keys only, so neither field is set.
